heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Observe
details: 1.1.1 Use relevant senses and suitable tools to observe objects, events or changes
1. Refer to Activity Book pp. 1–2 if available. Independently submit three property-and-sense pairs.
A fabric swatch, a wooden block, a closed shaker, pencils and a three-row observation table.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a swatch and a block. Ask which properties pupils can identify using sight or touch.
Describe one visible property and one property they can feel.
Main activity
Model one observation using “I notice … using …”. Guide pairs through three stations for sight, touch and hearing.
At each station, observe one item, record its property and name the sense used. Compare entries with a partner.
Practice and assessment
Check three entries per pupil for a property and a matching sense. Give prompts where an entry is a guess.
Refer to Activity Book pp. 1–2 if available. Independently submit three property-and-sense pairs.
Closure
Ask pupils to give one observation that another person could check.
Share a property and name how they checked it.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Observe
details: 1.1.1 Use relevant senses and suitable tools to observe objects, events or changes
1. Observe a leaf, smooth stone and cloth using sight and touch; record three observations and identify the sense used.
A fabric swatch, a wooden block, a closed shaker, pencils and a three-row observation table.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a leaf and a smooth stone. Ask which observations can be made without touching.
Name a visible feature of each object.
Targeted reinforcement / PBD
Provide clean safe objects, a recording sheet and a new observation task.
Observe a leaf, smooth stone and cloth using sight and touch; record three observations and identify the sense used.
Closure
Ask a pupil to read one observation and name the sense used.
State one recorded observation and the corresponding sense.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Classify
details: 1.1.2 Group objects or phenomena by similarities and differences
1. Refer to Activity Book pp. 3–4 if available. Individually sort the new pictures, then write or say the rule.
Animal picture cards and two sorting mats per pair. Use clear full-body pictures.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a duck and a goat. Ask pupils to identify a feature visible in one picture only.
Point to a feature and describe the difference.
Main activity
Model how one feature produces two groups. Give pairs six cards and ask them to check each card against their rule.
Sort the cards, label each group and explain one decision to a partner. Test a second feature if time permits.
Practice and assessment
Give pictures of a chicken, an owl, a parrot, a cat, a horse and a rabbit. Check that the labels express opposite outcomes of one visible feature and all six placements follow the rule.
Refer to Activity Book pp. 3–4 if available. Individually sort the new pictures, then write or say the rule.
Closure
Move one card to the wrong group and ask for a correction.
Move the card back and justify the placement using the feature.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Classify
details: 1.1.2 Group objects or phenomena by similarities and differences
1. Sort six new picture cards into groups using one observable feature; explain the rule and check an alternative grouping.
Animal picture cards and two sorting mats per pair. Use clear full-body pictures.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a round red card and a square red card. Ask for two possible sorting rules.
Suggest colour or shape as a sorting rule.
Targeted reinforcement / PBD
Give cards showing familiar animals or objects with clear visible characteristics.
Sort six new picture cards into groups using one observable feature; explain the rule and check an alternative grouping.
Closure
Show a new card and ask where it belongs under the chosen rule.
Place it in the appropriate group and state the rule.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Measure and Use Numbers
details: 1.1.3 Measure using suitable tools and techniques and record the results with numbers and units
1. Refer to Activity Book pp. 5–6 if available. Independently measure the two strips and label both readings with cm.
30 cm rulers, pre-cut strips in whole-centimetre lengths and a two-row recording table.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show two strips with different starting positions. Ask how to compare their lengths fairly.
Suggest lining up the ends and using the same ruler.
Main activity
Demonstrate aligning an end to the zero mark and reading the other end from above. Deliberately start at the 1 cm mark and ask pupils to identify the error.
Take turns measuring and checking with a partner. Record each length in a table with the unit cm.
Practice and assessment
Give each pupil two unmarked strips of 8 cm and 14 cm. Check ruler placement and both readings.
Refer to Activity Book pp. 5–6 if available. Independently measure the two strips and label both readings with cm.
Closure
Ask what information is missing if a measurement is written as “12”.
Give the unit and explain where to place the strip to start.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Communicate
details: 1.1.4 Record and share information or ideas in a suitable form
1. Refer to Activity Book pp. 7–8 if available. Convert the tally into a labelled table independently, then report the red and blue totals and say which colour has more.
Bags of coloured counters, tally sheets and pencils.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show an unlabelled tally. Ask what a reader needs to know to interpret it.
Suggest labels for what was counted and the number counted.
Main activity
Pre-sort counter sets and give each pair a printed table. Give groups counters in three colours. Model the first table row and ask how the row helps a listener understand the findings.
Count the counters, agree on totals and take turns explaining a finding using their table.
Practice and assessment
Give each pupil a new tally showing four red, six blue and two yellow counters. Check the headings, the red and blue totals, and the comparison.
Refer to Activity Book pp. 7–8 if available. Convert the tally into a labelled table independently, then report the red and blue totals and say which colour has more.
Closure
Ask what would make a classmate's table easy to understand.
Identify one useful feature, such as clear category headings.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Use Apparatus and Handle Specimens / Sketch and Clean Apparatus
details:
1.2.1 Use and handle science apparatus and materials using the correct methods
1.2.2 Handle specimens carefully and appropriately
1.2.3 Draw accurate sketches of specimens, apparatus and science materials
1.2.4 Clean science apparatus using the correct method
TB pp. 12–14 · AB pp. 9–10 (shared section · reference)

1. Independently prepare one cup, then explain how the dropper or tweezers helped. Refer to the relevant items in Activity Book pp. 9–10 if available.
2. Sketch and label the setup independently. Clean the used cup and dropper, then show both items to the teacher.

Water, plastic droppers, shallow clear cups, cotton wool, dried beans, blunt tweezers and trays. Tell pupils the beans are for observation.; A clear plastic cup with a bean and damp cotton wool, plastic dropper, shallow tray, clean rinse water and a draining rack. Prepare a second cup and dropper used with water and a pinch of sugar for cleaning practice.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show two prepared cups, one with damp cotton wool and one with pooled water. Ask which tool helps control the amount.
Choose a dropper and describe the difference between the cups.
Main activity
Set up individual trays with cotton wool, droppers and blunt tweezers. Demonstrate drawing water into the dropper and adding it a few drops at a time. Show how to lift a bean gently over the tray.
Take turns preparing a cup. Stop when the cotton wool is evenly damp and place two beans apart so both can be seen.
Practice and assessment
Give each pupil a clean setup and check dropper use, absence of pooled water, and careful transfer of both seeds.
Independently prepare one cup, then explain how the dropper or tweezers helped. Refer to the relevant items in Activity Book pp. 9–10 if available.
Closure
Ask how to correct a setup with too much water.
Explain how adding a few drops at a time prevents pooling.
Set induction
Show a simple line drawing of a cup and ask what would make the specimen inside easy to identify.
Suggest showing the bean outline and adding a clear label.
Main activity
Prepare used cups, rinse water and a drying rack at each table. Model drawing from the side, then show how to rinse a used cup and draw and expel clean water through the dropper over the tray.
Practise sketching the cup setup with a partner. Take turns rinsing the used cup and dropper and placing them on the rack.
Practice and assessment
Check each pupil's sketch for a clear outline and correct labels for the cup, bean and cotton wool. Observe each pupil rinsing both items and checking for residue.
Sketch and label the setup independently. Clean the used cup and dropper, then show both items to the teacher.
Closure
Ask why a dropper used for sugar solution still needs rinsing if the liquid looks clear.
Explain that clear liquid can still contain dissolved sugar, then describe how to rinse the dropper.
references: TB pp. 12–14 · AB pp. 9–10 (shared section · reference)

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Store Apparatus and Substances
details: 1.2.5 Store science apparatus and materials properly and safely
TB pp. 12–14 · AB pp. 9–10 (shared section · reference)
1. Put the three items away independently. Point to the drying rack and explain when the wet cup can be stored.
A clean dry plastic cup, a clean dry plastic dropper, a closed labelled container of table sugar, a wet cup, an equipment tray, a substance shelf and a drying rack.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a wet cup beside a dry cup. Ask which is ready to put away.
Choose the dry cup and give one reason.
Main activity
Label storage locations and lay out the three dry items. Model checking that apparatus is clean and dry and that the substance lid is closed. Point out the storage labels and drying rack.
In pairs, check sample items, choose the correct location and explain why a wet item goes to the rack.
Practice and assessment
Observe each pupil returning a dry cup, a dry dropper and the closed sugar container. Check all three locations and the response to the wet cup.
Put the three items away independently. Point to the drying rack and explain when the wet cup can be stored.
Closure
Ask what to check before returning the sugar container.
Check the label and confirm that the lid is closed.
references: TB pp. 12–14 · AB pp. 9–10 (shared section · reference)

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Follow Science Room Rules
details: 2.1.1 Follow the rules for working in the science room
1. Clean and return assigned equipment independently. Explain to the teacher or write how a clear walkway or immediate reporting keeps people safe.
Plastic cups, plastic spoons, water, trays, cleaning cloths, incident picture cards and a pupil checklist. Use a picture to simulate a spill or damaged item.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Mark the bag area and show how to keep the walkway clear. Record each pupil's entry action on the checklist.
Leave bags in the agreed area, walk to the assigned station and wait for instructions.
Main activity
Demonstrate transferring a spoonful of water between cups over a tray. Show an incident card to one group at a time and observe how each pupil reports it.
Take turns moving water over the tray. When shown an incident card, stop, leave the affected item alone and tell the teacher where it is and what happened.
Practice and assessment
Observe each pupil clean and return one item. Use three checklist columns for entry, reporting and clean-up. Recheck an action after a short prompt where needed.
Clean and return assigned equipment independently. Explain to the teacher or write how a clear walkway or immediate reporting keeps people safe.
Closure
Review the response to a damaged item and ask which action to take first.
State the first action. Use Activity Book pp. 11–12 for follow-up if available.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Human Reproduction
details: 3.1.1 State that humans reproduce by giving birth
1. Independently select the newborn picture and answer the second question in a sentence.
Teacher-made cards showing a newborn with a caregiver, an older child, and an unrelated picture of an egg hatching.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a picture of a newborn with a caregiver. Ask which person has just been born.
Point to the newborn and describe what they see.
Main activity
Display the three picture choices together for a quick response. Introduce the words human, newborn and giving birth. Compare the two human cards and ask which represents the arrival of a new baby.
Sort the pictures, match the newborn card to the phrase “giving birth” and say how humans reproduce.
Practice and assessment
Show three new drawings: a newborn with a caregiver, a child reading and a chick hatching. Ask “Which drawing shows a human who has just been born?” and “How do humans reproduce?”
Independently select the newborn picture and answer the second question in a sentence.
Closure
Ask for the key sentence again and connect it to the next lesson on changes after birth.
State that humans reproduce by giving birth.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Describe Growth Since Birth
details: 3.1.2 Describe how a person's size, height and weight change as they grow from birth
1. Independently describe the changes in body size, height and weight. Cite one pair of readings as evidence.
Stage cards and a fictional record showing 50 cm and 3 kg at birth and 120 cm and 23 kg at age seven, with two illustrations of the same child.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show the child's two pictures. Ask how the earlier and later stages differ.
Identify the baby and the older child and name one visible change.
Main activity
Model reading a two-row growth record. Ask which column shows height and which shows weight. Use pictures to discuss body size.
Put the stage cards in order and use the record and pictures to make one statement about each change.
Practice and assessment
Give a new fictional example, with 49 cm and 3 kg at birth and 117 cm and 21 kg at age seven. Check all three statements against the pictures and record.
Independently describe the changes in body size, height and weight. Cite one pair of readings as evidence.
Closure
Ask how to distinguish what was seen in the picture from what was read in the record.
Identify the evidence used for body size and for one measured change.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Compare Growth Among Individuals
details: 3.1.3 Use activity findings to conclude that individuals grow differently
1. Measure the outlines, compare the recorded changes in height of both children and conclude that individuals grow differently.
Teacher-made paper hand outlines with pre-checked lengths, rulers and anonymised model records. Do not collect pupils' own body measurements.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show two different hand outlines labelled “Age 7”. Ask whether equal age means equal size.
Suggest a measurement that could test the idea.
Main activity
Model measuring hand length from the wrist line to the longest fingertip. Give pairs dated records of two same-age children at two ages and their matching hand outlines.
Measure the outlines, compare the recorded changes in height of both children and conclude that individuals grow differently.
Closure
Ask which measurement on the group's chart is about height and which is about hand length.
Point to one value of each kind and state that growth can differ.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Compare Growth Among Individuals / Recognise Inherited Features
details:
3.1.3 Use activity findings to conclude that individuals grow differently
3.1.4 Describe how offspring inherit features from parents or earlier generations
3.1.5 Give examples of inherited features such as skin colour, iris colour and hair type
TB pp. 28–30 · AB p. 16 · TB pp. 30–32 · AB pp. 17–20 (shared section · reference)

1. Independently measure the outlines and write one comparison about hand length, one about height and one conclusion.
2. Independently name two possible inherited features, identify the people who share them and explain the idea in one sentence.

Teacher-made paper hand outlines with pre-checked lengths, rulers and anonymised model records. Do not collect pupils' own body measurements.; Illustrated fictional family charts and feature cards for iris colour, hair type and skin colour.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Display the two recorded heights and hand lengths from the preceding activity.
Identify which quantities are being compared.
Practice and assessment
Give a fresh pair of outlines measuring 12 cm and 14 cm, with heights of 123 cm and 118 cm. Check two accurate comparisons and an evidence-based conclusion.
Independently measure the outlines and write one comparison about hand length, one about height and one conclusion.
Closure
Ask what the examples show about children of the same age.
Explain that their measurements can differ and point to one result.
Set induction
Show two fictional relatives with the same hair type. Ask pupils to describe the feature.
Describe the shared hair type using the illustration.
Main activity

Use one enlarged fictional chart and preprinted individual charts. Model reading a fictional family chart across two generations. Explain that a shared feature may be inherited and that a picture alone cannot tell which relative it came from.
Circle two shared features and discuss why clothing or a hairstyle chosen for the day is a different kind of similarity.
Practice and assessment
Give a fictional chart showing that Aina and her mother have brown irises, and Aina and her grandfather have wavy hair. Check both examples and the explanation.
Independently name two possible inherited features, identify the people who share them and explain the idea in one sentence.
Closure
Ask for one feature pupils can compare on a chart.
Name a feature and point to an example in the fictional chart.
references: TB pp. 28–30 · AB p. 16 · TB pp. 30–32 · AB pp. 17–20 (shared section · reference)

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Communicate Findings About Growth and Heredity
details: 3.1.6 Explain observations about growth and heredity using drawings, digital tools, writing or speech
1. Independently present both findings through a labelled sketch, two short written statements or an oral explanation.
Case cards with two dated height readings and a fictional family illustration, pencils and a two-box response sheet.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a height record and a fictional family chart. Ask which source answers a question about change over time.
Choose the height record and explain why it has two readings.
Main activity

Prepare the height record and family chart on one response slip. Model a growth statement supported by two readings and an inheritance statement supported by a shared feature. Offer a labelled sketch or short oral report.
Prepare a two-part explanation with a partner and check that the evidence matches each statement.
Practice and assessment
Give a new case with heights of 104 cm and 121 cm and a chart showing shared curly hair. Check one supported finding of each type.
Independently present both findings through a labelled sketch, two short written statements or an oral explanation.
Closure
Ask pupils to name the evidence that makes one of their statements clear.
Point to the two readings or the shared feature in the chart.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Scientific skills, safety and human growth / How Animals Reproduce
details:
1.1 Science process skills
1.2 Manipulative skills
2.1 Science room rules
3.1 Human reproduction and growth
4.1 Animal reproduction and growth

1.1.2 Group objects or phenomena by similarities and differences
1.2.1 Use and handle science apparatus and materials using the correct methods
2.1.1 Follow the rules for working in the science room
3.1.2 Describe how a person's size, height and weight change as they grow from birth
4.1.1 State the ways animals reproduce
Teacher-prepared task · TB pp. 36–37 · AB pp. 21–22 (shared section · reference)

1. Sort and label the groups, show a safe transfer and explain one change such as becoming taller.
2. Independently write or say “lays eggs” and “gives birth to live young”, then match them to the duck and elephant.

Object cards, a plastic dropper, water, an empty tray and child-growth cards.; Picture pairs showing a duck with eggs and a goat with its young, plus picture cards of a crocodile nest and an elephant calf.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show two objects and ask which visible property could group them.
Describe a property that can be checked.
Main activity
Model one sorting rule, safe dropper use over a tray, and ordering baby and child pictures.
Sort cards using one rule, move water in drops and describe a change as a child grows.
Practice and assessment
Give a new set of four cards. Check the stated rule and four placements, safe transfer of water, and one valid growth change.
Sort and label the groups, show a safe transfer and explain one change such as becoming taller.
Closure
Ask where the dropper should be placed after use.
Point to the tray and leave it ready for the next pupil.
Set induction
Show a duckling and a kid. Ask how each came into the world.
Make a prediction for each animal.
Main activity

Hand out one set of animal picture cards per pair. Reveal the picture evidence and model the phrases “lays eggs” and “gives birth to live young”. Introduce the crocodile and elephant cards and ask which phrase fits each.
Match a phrase to each picture pair and explain their choices to a partner.
Practice and assessment
Hand out an exit slip showing a duck and an elephant with their young. Ask pupils to state the two ways and label each example.
Independently write or say “lays eggs” and “gives birth to live young”, then match them to the duck and elephant.
Closure
Ask for one example of each way and point to the matching pictures.
State the two examples in full sentences.
references: Teacher-prepared task · TB pp. 36–37 · AB pp. 21–22 (shared section · reference)

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Classify Animals by Reproduction
details: 4.1.2 Group animals by whether they lay eggs or give birth
TB pp. 36–38 · AB pp. 21–22 (shared section · reference)
1. Sort the cards, then swap one example with another team and explain its placement.
Two-column sorting mat and illustrated clues for duck, crocodile, mosquito, goat, bat and elephant.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Hold up a bat and a duck card. Ask what evidence would tell us how each reproduces.
Suggest looking for eggs or evidence of a live birth.
Main activity
Model sorting a duck using a picture of its nest. Give teams the clue cards and ask them to read the evidence before they place each animal.
Sort the cards, then swap one example with another team and explain its placement.
Closure
Show a chick and a kitten card and ask how each starts life.
Identify which comes from an egg and which is born alive.
references: TB pp. 36–38 · AB pp. 21–22 (shared section · reference)

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Classify Animals by Reproduction / Animals That Lay Few or Many Eggs
details:
4.1.2 Group animals by whether they lay eggs or give birth
4.1.3 Give examples of animals that lay relatively few or many eggs
TB pp. 36–38 · AB pp. 21–22 (shared section · reference) · TB pp. 39–40 · AB p. 23

1. Independently place the animals in the two groups and explain one choice using its clue.
2. Independently name the animals, use “few” or “many” for each and refer to the eggs shown.

Two-column sorting mat and illustrated clues for duck, crocodile, mosquito, goat, bat and elephant.; Swan nest and frogspawn illustrations, counters for the swan nest, and an illustrated observation sheet with a swan and a fish example.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show two new cards, a duck and a cat, before returning the classification sheets.
Predict their groups and explain the evidence needed.
Practice and assessment
Give each pupil a shuffled six-card sheet with short clues. Check for at least five correct placements and one justification.
Independently place the animals in the two groups and explain one choice using its clue.
Closure
Ask why a duck and a bat can both fly and still belong in different groups.
Identify the way each reproduces as the sorting rule.
Set induction
Display a swan nest and a frogspawn picture side by side. Ask which has more visible eggs.
Point to the picture with more eggs and describe the clue.
Main activity

Use ready-printed nest and egg-cluster observations; compare side by side. Use counters to represent the eggs in the illustrated swan nest. Show a large cluster of frog eggs and ask pupils to compare the observations.
Make a sketch of each observation and describe which animal laid few eggs and which laid many in the examples.
Practice and assessment
Give pupils a swan-nest illustration and a fish-egg cluster with the animal named. Check one evidence-based sentence for each picture.
Independently name the animals, use “few” or “many” for each and refer to the eggs shown.
Closure
Ask for one pair of examples from the lesson.
Compare the swan and frog examples in one sentence.
references: TB pp. 36–38 · AB pp. 21–22 (shared section · reference) · TB pp. 39–40 · AB p. 23

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Animals That Give Birth to Few or Many Young
details: 4.1.4 Give examples of animals that give birth to relatively few or many young
1. Independently write or say that the dolphin is the “few” example and the cat is the “many” example, citing the two counts.
Model birth records for an elephant with one calf, a rabbit with six kits, a dolphin with one calf and a cat with five kittens.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show an elephant birth record and ask how many young were born in that record.
Count the calf and state the number.
Main activity
Provide the four illustrated birth records in a two-column format. Compare the elephant record with the rabbit record. Ask what the two examples show about the number born at a time.
Fill a two-row table with animal, number born and “few” or “many”. Explain the comparison to a partner.
Practice and assessment
Give the dolphin and cat records. Ask pupils to compare them and check the names and evidence.
Independently write or say that the dolphin is the “few” example and the cat is the “many” example, citing the two counts.
Closure
Ask what pupils looked at to decide between “few” and “many”.
State that they compared how many young were born in the examples.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Record Changes During Animal Growth
details: 4.1.5 Observe animal life cycles and record changes as animals grow
1. Independently number the stages and record two changes using arrows, labelled sketches or short phrases.
Frog and cow life-cycle illustrations, four shuffled frog cards and a recording strip.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a tadpole and an adult frog. Ask pupils to point to one visible difference.
Describe a feature such as the tail or legs.
Main activity
Model how to record the appearance of a stage from an illustration. Use calf and adult cow illustrations to practise recording an observation, then distribute the frog cards.
Sequence frog eggs, tadpole, froglet and adult frog. Discuss the froglet’s legs and the shorter tail, then compare the froglet with the adult frog.
Practice and assessment
Hand out a fresh four-image frog strip in a different order. Check the sequence and two changes between neighbouring stages.
Independently number the stages and record two changes using arrows, labelled sketches or short phrases.
Closure
Ask which pair of images supports one change.
Point to two stages and read out the change.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Compare Young Animals and Their Adults
details: 4.1.6 Use examples to explain which young animals resemble their parents and which look different
1. Match young animals to their adults and mark a visible similarity or difference on each pair.
Paired pictures of a kitten and adult cat, a calf and adult cow, a caterpillar and adult butterfly, and a tadpole and adult frog.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show the kitten and adult cat. Ask which features can be seen on both.
Identify a shared feature such as four legs.
Main activity
Model using the same feature to compare both pictures. Contrast the adult butterfly's wings with the caterpillar picture.
Match young animals to their adults and mark a visible similarity or difference on each pair.
Closure
Show an adult frog and a tadpole and ask about a visible difference.
Name one difference in body form.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Compare Young Animals and Their Adults / Communicate Observations About Reproduction and Growth
details:
4.1.6 Use examples to explain which young animals resemble their parents and which look different
4.1.7 Explain observations about animal reproduction and growth using drawings, digital tools, writing or speech
TB pp. 43–44 · AB p. 28 · TB p. 46 and p. 48 · Teacher-made assessment

1. Independently explain how the calf resembles the cow and how the tadpole differs from the adult frog.
2. Independently communicate that the adult lays eggs, that a caterpillar hatches and that an adult with wings emerges from the chrysalis, or give other supported observations.

Paired pictures of a kitten and adult cat, a calf and adult cow, a caterpillar and adult butterfly, and a tadpole and adult frog.; Butterfly life-cycle pictures showing an adult laying eggs, a caterpillar, a chrysalis and an adult butterfly, plus paper for labelled sketches.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Display an adult cow with its calf and an adult frog with its tadpole.
Point to one similar or different feature before the recorded comparison.
Practice and assessment
Give pupils the cow and frog pairs. Check one comparison supported by a feature for each pair.
Independently explain how the calf resembles the cow and how the tadpole differs from the adult frog.
Closure
Ask for one example of a young animal that looks noticeably different from its adult.
Name the example and point to the feature that supports it.
Set induction
Show a butterfly laying eggs and ask pupils which detail tells us how it reproduces.
Point to the eggs and describe what the adult does.
Main activity

Pre-arrange the life-cycle pictures; allow oral reports alongside sketches. Demonstrate how to mark the reproduction observation separately from changes in growth on a simple picture sequence. Give pairs a set of cycle pictures.
Rehearse a short report with a partner. Point to the egg-laying image and explain two changes shown across the pictures.
Practice and assessment
Invite each pupil to make a labelled sketch, write a short report or give an oral account. Check the reproduction observation and two growth observations against the pictures.
Independently communicate that the adult lays eggs, that a caterpillar hatches and that an adult with wings emerges from the chrysalis, or give other supported observations.
Closure
Invite one pupil to share an observation and show its evidence.
Listen and locate the matching picture.
references: TB pp. 43–44 · AB p. 28 · TB p. 46 and p. 48 · Teacher-made assessment

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Explain Why Plants Are Important
details: 5.1.1 State how plants are important to people and animals
1. Independently write or say that the mango tree provides food for a person and that the tree provides shelter for the bird.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan

details: 6.1.2 Compare activities carried out in light and dark conditions

Identical enclosed viewing boxes with the same arrangement of four large symbols, torch mounted on one box, second symbol set, recording slips and a picture of a reader.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a picture of someone trying to read a sign when a light is off. Ask pupils what would help.
Suggest turning on a light and predict how it will affect reading.
Main activity

Prepare paired viewing boxes and equivalent symbols before the lesson; run trials concurrently. Use a lit and an unlit box while the classroom remains lit. Count how many symbols they can identify correctly in each condition and record both observations. Compare their results with a partner.
Practice and assessment
Give a sample result of four correct in the lit box and one in the unlit box. Ask each pupil to interpret the evidence and apply it to reading the sign.
Independently identify the easier condition, cite both results and explain why the sign is easier to read when lit.

Ask why both viewing times should match.
Explain that keeping the time the same makes the comparison about the light.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK

activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Shine a torch onto a screen and ask where to place a card to darken part of the screen.

Keep the screen and torch fixed. Ask pairs to put the card between them, then off to one side. Keep the torch aimed at the screen.
Test both positions, draw the arrangement and record whether a shadow appears on the screen.

Give diagrams with the card in the beam and to the side. Ask pupils to mark the shadow position and explain it.
Independently identify the in-beam arrangement, shade the region behind the card on the screen and explain that the card blocks light.

Ask what happens to the shadow when the card is removed.
Predict that the patch disappears as light reaches the screen again.

activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils

Ask pupils to point to the material that produced the most distinct outline on their screen.

Give fresh pictures of grit mixed with large beads, steel clips mixed with plastic pieces, and cork mixed with stones in water. Ask pupils to explain each choice.

Ask why a magnet did not help with cork and stones.
Explain that the chosen materials do not respond to the classroom magnet and recall the property that did help.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Investigate Which Materials Dissolve in Water
details: 8.1.3 Investigate which materials dissolve in water
1. Independently record four observations, then use them to group sugar and salt together and sand and rice together.
Four labelled clear cups, equal water portions, small measured amounts of sugar, salt, sand and rice, separate stirrers and a results table.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show salt before and after it dissolves in a glass. Ask whether the salt is still present.
Describe what can be seen and suggest that the salt is mixed into the water.
Main activity
Use equal volumes, small portions of each material, equal stirring and the same observation time. Check that pupils record particles that settle as still visible.
Test each sample, note whether particles remain, and compare results with a partner.
Practice and assessment
Ask each pupil for an observation and classification in each row. Check that sugar and salt have dissolved and that sand and rice remain visible in the prepared test.
Independently record four observations, then use them to group sugar and salt together and sand and rice together.
Closure
Ask what happened to the salt when it could no longer be seen.
Explain that it dissolved and remained mixed in the water.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Investigate the Effect of Water Temperature
details: 8.1.4 Use investigation results to explain how to make a material dissolve faster
1. Record the dissolving times and use the results to explain which water temperature makes sugar dissolve faster.
Clear cups, cool water and teacher-prepared comfortably warm water, equal masses of the same sugar, identical stirrers, timer and record slips.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show the two cups and ask which condition might make the same sugar dissolve sooner.
Predict the result and identify the temperature difference.
Main activity
Prepare safe warm and room-temperature water with equal volumes and equal sugar masses. Keep grain size and stirring constant, time both trials and compare the results.
Record the dissolving times and use the results to explain which water temperature makes sugar dissolve faster.
Closure
Display both recorded dissolving times.
Identify the shorter time and its corresponding cup.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Investigate the Effect of Water Temperature / Investigate the Effect of Stirring
details: 8.1.4 Use investigation results to explain how to make a material dissolve faster
TB pp. 96–97 · AB p. 59 (temperature · comparison) · TB pp. 97–98 · AB p. 61

1. Independently report both readings and say which condition dissolved the sugar sooner in the trial.
2. Record the visible grains at the same times and explain from the results whether stirring makes salt dissolve faster.

Clear cups, cool water and teacher-prepared comfortably warm water, equal masses of the same sugar, identical stirrers, timer and record slips.; Two clear cups, equal portions of water and table salt, stirrer, timer and a two-column observation slip.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Return the two temperature-test records and ask which cup dissolved sugar sooner.
Point to the recorded time supporting the answer.
Practice and assessment
Ask pupils to write both times, circle the shorter one and make a conclusion about temperature. Check the conclusion against the trial records.
Independently report both readings and say which condition dissolved the sugar sooner in the trial.
Closure
Ask why using more sugar in one cup would affect the comparison.
Explain that both cups need the same amount so that temperature is the difference being tested.
Set induction
Show a spoon beside a cup with salt at the bottom. Ask how to check whether stirring makes a difference.
Suggest comparing one stirred cup with a second cup left still.
Main activity
Keep water temperature, volume and salt mass the same. Stir one cup steadily and leave the other still. Ask groups to observe at the same intervals and compare the recorded outcomes.
Record the visible grains at the same times and explain from the results whether stirring makes salt dissolve faster.
Closure
Ask which two observations must be compared at the same time point.
Point to the corresponding stirred and unstirred entries.
references: TB pp. 96–97 · AB p. 59 (temperature · comparison) · TB pp. 97–98 · AB p. 61

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK

details: 8.1.4 Use investigation results to explain how to make a material dissolve faster

Two clear cups, equal portions of water and table salt, stirrer, timer and a two-column observation slip.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show the stirring experiment's paired observations at one time point.
Identify where more grains remained visible before drawing a conclusion.

Ask pupils to record both observations at a time when the cups differ and explain which sample dissolved faster. Repeat the demonstration if the first trial gives no clear comparison.
Independently cite what remained visible in each cup and draw a conclusion about stirring.
Closure
Ask why the group observed both cups at the same times.
Explain that a comparison needs observations from the same stage of the test.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Investigate the Effect of Particle Size
details: 8.1.4 Use investigation results to explain how to make a material dissolve faster
1. Independently make the comparison and explain that the finer sugar dissolved sooner when the measurements support it.
Equal masses of sugar prepared from two identical cubes, one crushed finer than the other, clear cups, water, stirrers, timer and a record sheet.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Display the two sugar portions and ask what is different and what has stayed the same.
Identify the different particle sizes and confirm that the portions have the same mass.

Keep water volume and temperature fixed. Have both pupils stir at the same pace and start timing together. Check that they use the same endpoint.
Time each sample until the grains are no longer visible and record both results.
Practice and assessment
Ask each pupil to report the two times, choose the faster sample and identify one factor kept the same.
Independently make the comparison and explain that the finer sugar dissolved sooner when the measurements support it.
Closure
Ask what the test would show if the finer sample also used much warmer water.
Explain that the effects of temperature and particle size would be mixed.

Ask pupils to point to one part of a response that gives evidence.
Identify a detail that supports their explanation.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan

details: 9.1.1 Identify natural water sources such as rain, rivers, lakes, seas and springs

Pupils

Explain that spring water comes out of the ground and rain falls from clouds.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Observe the Direction of Water Flow
details: 9.1.2 Use activities to identify the direction in which water flows

1. Independently draw both arrows towards the lower ends and explain that the water changed direction when the high end changed.

Shallow trays, small cups of coloured water, stable blocks, cloths and two-diagram response slips.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a tray raised at one end. Ask where a small amount of water is likely to collect.
Point to a predicted end and explain the choice using height.
Main activity
Prepare the two tray setups and water in small cups before class. Guide groups to release water near the high end, record what happens and then reverse which end is raised.
Observe and sketch the flow in both setups. Compare where the water collects each time.
Practice and assessment
Give two tray diagrams with opposite slopes. Ask pupils to mark arrows and support their rule with a trial observation.
Independently draw both arrows towards the lower ends and explain that the water changed direction when the high end changed.
Targeted reinforcement / PBD
Use shallow trays and small amounts of water; wipe spills immediately.
Compare water flowing down two differently tilted trays; draw arrows and identify the higher and lower ends.
Closure
Ask whether water always flows to the right in this investigation.
Refer to the two trials and state that the direction depends on which end is lower.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Explain How Rivers and Waterfalls Flow
details: 9.1.3 Use observations from different media to describe how water flows naturally in rivers and waterfalls
1. Independently draw both arrows from higher to lower ground and state the common direction of natural water flow.
Waterfall photograph, river landscape diagram with marked heights, two new sketch cards and pencils.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a waterfall photograph and ask where the water starts and lands.
Identify the top and the pool below and point to the direction of movement.

Use two large ready-drawn landscape diagrams and a response slip. Compare the photograph with a river diagram showing a hillside and a lowland. Turn the diagram so the downhill path points the opposite way on the page.
Trace the water in each representation and explain what stays the same when the diagram is turned.

Provide a new waterfall sketch and a river sketch with high and low points. Check both arrows and a sentence supported by the examples.
Independently draw both arrows from higher to lower ground and state the common direction of natural water flow.

Ask which clue is more useful, the side of the page or the height of the land.
Choose the land height and justify it with one example.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Sequence the Natural Water Cycle
details: 9.1.4 Put the stages of the natural water cycle in order
1. Independently order and label the four stages and complete the circular path.
Cards for surface water, water vapour, clouds and rain, arrow cards and blank cycle mats.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a picture of a puddle becoming smaller on a sunny day. Ask what may happen to some of the water.
Suggest that some water changes to vapour and mixes with the air.

Model arranging surface water, water vapour, clouds and rain. Explain that vapour cools into tiny droplets that form clouds and that rain returns water to rivers and seas.

Provide a shuffled four-stage set. Check the order and direction of each arrow, including the return from rain to surface water.
Independently order and label the four stages and complete the circular path.

Ask whether the cycle has to start with the sea in every diagram.
Point to a different starting stage and trace the same order around the cycle.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Explain Observations About the Water Cycle
details: 9.1.5 Explain observations about the water cycle using drawings, digital tools, writing or speech
1. Independently explain that vapour cooled into droplets on the underside and that larger drops fell, like rain returning water to the surface.
Teacher-prepared clear bowl with comfortably warm water, clear cover cooled on top with an ice pack, response sheets.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a dry clear cover and ask pupils to predict where water might appear when it covers the bowl.
Make a prediction and identify the surface they will observe.

Prepare the covered bowl and external ice pack early enough for droplets to be observable. Keep the ice pack outside the covered bowl and point out droplets forming underneath. Observe droplets gathering and falling, then discuss how the cooled cover represents cooling in the air.

Ask for a labelled sketch, short caption or oral response giving both observations and their links to the natural cycle.
Independently explain that vapour cooled into droplets on the underside and that larger drops fell, like rain returning water to the surface.

Ask why the class used a dry cover at the start.
Explain that it helps establish that the droplets formed during the demonstration.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK

details: 9.2.1 State that air is present around us

1. Independently state that air is around us, then explain that it filled the bag and occupied space in the inverted cup.

Clear cups, water basin, dry tissue, small clear bag and observation slips.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Hold up a limp clear bag, sweep it through the room and close it. Ask what made it expand.
Observe the change and suggest that air entered the bag.
Main activity

Prepare the tissue cup and water tray before class; demonstrate both trials. Put tissue in the top of an inverted cup and lower it straight into water. Tilt the cup in a second trial so bubbles escape and water enters.
Compare both trials, observe the bubbles and describe how the air affected the water entering the cup.
Practice and assessment
Ask each pupil to state where the air came from in the bag and what the cup experiment showed. Check both explanations against the observations.
Independently state that air is around us, then explain that it filled the bag and occupied space in the inverted cup.

Demonstrate the two observations with safe classroom materials; ask pupils to point to evidence of air, without requiring explanations of pressure.
Observe an inverted transparent cup trapping air above water and a bag filled with air from the classroom. Identify evidence that air is present around us.
Closure
Ask what the bubbles showed when the cup was tilted.
Explain that some air left the cup and moved through the water.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Name Gases Found in Air
details: 9.2.2 State that air contains gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide
1. Independently name oxygen and carbon dioxide, state that air contains several gases and select oxygen for breathing.
Air-mixture diagram, gas word cards, breathing illustration and individual response slips.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a picture of a child breathing outdoors. Ask whether air is made of one gas or several.
Share a prediction and name any gas they already know.

Print the air-mixture diagram and two gas labels for each pair. Use a diagram that labels oxygen and carbon dioxide alongside other gases. Explain that oxygen is needed for breathing and that the air we breathe out still contains several gases.
Place the two gas labels in the air diagram and explain why the names do not describe all of the air.

Ask pupils to complete a short air-mixture statement, name two example gases and identify the gas people need for breathing.
Independently name oxygen and carbon dioxide, state that air contains several gases and select oxygen for breathing.

Ask whether a bag filled with ordinary air contains only oxygen.
Explain that oxygen is one of several gases in the bag.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK

details:

Card fans, paper streamers, stands and individual comparison slips.
activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show a hanging streamer before and after waving a card fan. Ask what changed without touching the streamer.

Ask each pupil to describe both signs and state what wind means. Check the link between the moving air and each observation.

Use safe distances from fan blades or a hand fan only.
Observe a paper strip moved by a hand fan and a ribbon near a fan; record two signs of moving air and identify wind.

Ask what pupils observed when the fan was held still.
Explain that the streamer stopped moving after the airflow from the fan stopped.

heading: Daily Lesson Plan
Science (DLP) · Year 2 SK
Explain How Wind Affects Daily Life
details: 9.2.4 Suggest ways in which moving air affects everyday life

activities: Phase
Teacher
Pupils
Set induction
Show clothes on a line and ask how a breeze can affect them.
Suggest an effect and point to a clue in the picture.

Display the three daily-life pictures side by side. Compare a helpful breeze with strong winds in several settings. Model a sentence linking moving air to a visible change.
Sort situations by effect and explain how air can move a sail or help dry laundry, and how strong wind can damage property.

Give pictures of a sailboat, damp cloth and trees beside a roof during strong wind. Check two useful effects and one harmful effect with a reason for each.

Ask how the same moving air can be useful in one situation and harmful in another.
Compare a gentle breeze and a strong wind using one example of each.

Use a small preassembled model and labelled compartments; check each pupil's actual disassembly. Demonstrate working backwards through the assembly pictures. Model sorting the removed pieces, checking counts and placing each type in its labelled compartment.
Practise the reverse sequence and compare sorted groups with the inventory before storing them.
Practice and assessment
Observe each pupil disassemble a small model. Check the first part removed, the sorting, the inventory check and the final compartment placement.
Independently remove the pieces in order, sort and count them, then place them in their compartments and report a discrepancy if one appears.
Closure
Ask what to do if the count is one short.
Recheck the tray and work area, then tell the teacher which piece is missing.
